title: Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from overdose of fentanyl and other drugs
description: Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed b
body: Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina. The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death. Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence. The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse. The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions. Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addictionFentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone. The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful". The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death.Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died.Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression. Panettiere has said she was introduced to drugs around the age of 16 during a red carpet appearance for Heroes when a member of her professional team gave her something called a "happy pill" for energy."I had no idea that this was not an appropriate thing, or what door that would open for me when it came to my addiction," she told People Magazine. "As I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn't live without."Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition. Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother also struggled with substance abuse and used heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.

schema.headline: Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from overdose of fentanyl and other drugs

title: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences
description: Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police have said.The charges are an alle
body: Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police have said.The charges are an alleged indecent assault against a teenage girl aged 16 to 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham in 1991 and the alleged sexual assault of an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth in 2004.These charges are in addition to those brought against Westwood, 68, in October 2025 relating to seven women, which include four counts of rape.Westwood has previously denied multiple sex offences, including rape and sexual assault, and pleaded not guilty to earlier charges last December.Westwood is now facing a total of 17 charges involving nine women.Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police Service, said: "The women who have made reports have placed their trust in us, and we remain committed to providing them with all available support."Independent support is also available through Rape Crisis via its 24/7 Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line."Westwood is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court at a future date in relation to the two additional charges, the Met Police said.A trial relating to the original 15 charges is scheduled to begin at Southwark Crown Court on 25 January 2027.Catherine P Baccas, deputy chief crown prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) London, said: "Today the Crown Prosecution Service has authorised two further charges of sexual assault and indecent assault against Tim Westwood."Mr Westwood is already charged with nine counts of indecent assault, two counts of sexual assault and four counts of rape in relation to reported non-recent offences between 1983 and 2016 involving seven women."These new charges, following an investigation by the Metropolitan Police, relate to separate reports of non-recent offences in 1991 and 2004 involving two additional women."Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring these additional charges to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue further criminal proceedings."The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that criminal proceedings are active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial."

schema.headline: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences

title: New EU industry rules would damage UK, warns Andy Burnham
description: Andy Burnham has warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK, ahead of a meeting later with European Commission Pr
body: Andy Burnham has warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK, ahead of a meeting later with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies.The prime minister said he was concerned about how British industry and supply chains could be affected, and would raise the subject with von der Leyen when he meets her during a UN summit in New York.Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day".He said his immediate priority was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach an agreement that would boost the British economy. The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its supply chains. Tensions over the proposed scheme have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July.Burnham said: "We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us."We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain."We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies here… we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem."We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'."Burnham told reporters his own speech to the UN General Assembly later would reflect on the decade since the Brexit vote and the "turbulence comes when outside actors seek to manipulate, to distort facts, influence the British democratic process". "Going into the next decade, we need to be clear-eyed about that and become stronger and more on the front foot about challenging that," he said.Asked if he would rule out making a pledge to rejoin the EU at the next general election, Burnham said: "Our focus at the moment is on a UK-EU summit which we hope will take place later this year."My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir [Starmer] did in rebuilding bridges, because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade."He added: "What we have got to do is now go to the next level in terms of reaching practical agreement that will further boost the British economy, and those issues are the substance of the summit alongside EU requests around youth mobility."He said questions about rejoining the EU were for "another day". Speaking at the Liberal Democrat conference in Brighton on Monday, the EU's new ambassador to the UK was asked whether the UK could rejoin the EU or be granted associate membership.Jukka Salovaara said: "The doors are open but it's very much up to the UK public to identify and decide on its level of ambition when it comes to deepening cooperation with the EU." Last September, Burnham said he would like to see the UK back in the EU in his lifetime. Earlier this year, he said Brexit had been "damaging" but "the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments".  The EU has recently suggested Canada could become the bloc's first "associate member".Asked if this could be an option for the UK, Burnham said: "The European Union made it clear that that wasn't open to us."Additional reporting by Brian Wheeler

schema.headline: New EU industry rules would damage UK, warns Andy Burnham

title: Ed Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market
description: The Liberal Democrats will fight the next general election on a promise to cut taxes for millions of workers, Sir Ed Davey has said in a speech to his
body: The Liberal Democrats will fight the next general election on a promise to cut taxes for millions of workers, Sir Ed Davey has said in a speech to his party conference.The Lib Dem leader said that if he gained power, he would raise the annual tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.He would also raise the 40p income tax threshold from £50,270 to £56,000, in a £17bn package funded by the economic boost he says would come from the UK rejoining the EU single market and customs union.He claimed the plan would mean a £680 cut for "most taxpayers" but it would not come into full effect until the fifth year of a Lib Dem government - potentially up to eight years away. The announcement was greeted with sustained applause by Lib Dem MPs and activists in the Brighton conference centre.The £12,570 income tax allowance was frozen by the Conservatives in 2021, resulting in more people being dragged into paying the tax, and Labour has so far resisted calls from trade unions and some of its MPs to unfreeze it.The Lib Dems said they would raise the threshold to £15,000 a year, and increase the starting point for paying employee National Insurance (NI) to the same level.At their conference earlier this month, Reform UK promised to increase the income tax personal allowance to £15,000 within 100 days if they won power.Sir Ed told the Lib Dem faithful "the difference between us and Reform" is that "their tax cut is paid for through cruelty." He said "Reform's figures show they'd pay for it by ripping £22bn of crucial support away from disabled people."Under the Lib Dem plan, based on research by think tank Frontier Economics, external, the economic boost from rejoining the single market would allow the party to spend £17bn on tax cuts by the end of the next Parliament.The party says it would unfreeze personal allowances in the second year of a Lib Dem government, allowing them to rise with inflation, before bringing in big tax cuts in year five when the economic benefits of closer trading with the EU had kicked in.However, the move would depend on the party being able to negotiate a closer trading arrangement with the EU in just 12 months. Sir Ed has been under pressure this week to set out bolder policies, with his party languishing in fourth or fifth place in national opinion polls.He began his speech with a sombre and punchy attack on Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. He stopped short of calling Reform fascists, but drew a link between the fascists in Britain in the 1930s with what he called "thugs, in black shirts and balaclavas" in reference to the protests in Dover and Portsmouth in recent weeks."This is a far-right movement that is given oxygen, and heat, and fuel by politicians and parties who claim to be serious contenders to lead our country," said the Lib Dem leader.His solution is "community politics" that he argues is the hallmark of the Lib Dems."It will take more than a manifesto. It will take a movement, rooted in decency, fairness and community. British values. Liberal values," he said.Repositioning the Lib Dems as a tax cutting party is aimed at appealing to voters they are targeting in traditional Tory heartlands.And Sir Ed used his speech to attack Tory leader Kemi Badenoch over her policy shifts on climate change and human rights law."Millions of decent, moderate Conservative voters are getting her message, and they're turning away – increasingly, to us," he told the audience in Brighton.He took a swipe at Prime Minister Andy Burnham for failing to commit to rejoining the EU single market, something the Lib Dems say they would do in their first year in government.Lib Dem sources refused to say whether the income tax plan would be a condition of joining a coalition government with Labour or another party, saying the party's aim was to get as many MPs as possible.Sir Ed has ruled out a coalition with Reform UK, and dismissed suggestions he could do a deal with the Conservatives, as his party did in 2010.The Lib Dem leader also addressed the potential threat posed by AI in his speech, saying that "handled badly, it concentrates more power in fewer hands than at any point in human history."He said Burnham's AI partnership with US president Donald Trump "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of this threat" and called for "a global treaty to press pause on super-intelligent AI now".He proposed "a new International AI Safety Agency - like we have for nuclear - to stop anyone from developing this technology recklessly."

schema.headline: Ed Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market

title: Sri Lanka Easter attacks: Court finds 15 guilty over deadly bombings
description: Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured
body: Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.The court session was adjourned before sentencing.The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the High Court in the capital Colombo in two prison buses.Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children.They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo.The foreigners who died included 11 Indians, eight Britons and five Americans.Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there.In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities.In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks.Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions.For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks.The verdict comes as a separate investigation into former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists.The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics.Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations.Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations.

schema.headline: Sri Lanka Easter attacks: Court finds 15 guilty over deadly bombings

title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington made several attempts to convince the judge not to declare a mistrialByMa
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington made several attempts to convince the judge not to declare a mistrialByMadeline HalpertThe defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case.The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out. A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing". Figure caption, Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, LindsayWarning: This article contains distressing detailsThe juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this.Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home. Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children. In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated. Image source, The Heard FoundationImage caption, Cora, five, Callan, eight months, and Dawson, three He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires. In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her. Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him.The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial."If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote.Image source, @EdPaltzikImage caption, Desronvil (seen here in a photo provided by his lawyer) has said he had no doubt about Clancy's guiltSeveral jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News. The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

schema.headline: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone

title: Juvenile murder sentence rule doesn't breach human rights, says Supreme Court
description: Image source, Norfolk PoliceImage caption, Jesse Quaye (left) and Ayomindy Bile were sentenced to serve a minimum of 15 years for murderByHome and leg
body: Image source, Norfolk PoliceImage caption, Jesse Quaye (left) and Ayomindy Bile were sentenced to serve a minimum of 15 years for murderByHome and legal correspondentScrapping a law that could have shortened a man's prison sentence because he committed murder as a child was not a breach of human rights, the Supreme Court has ruled.Jesse Quaye, then 17, and Ayomindy Bile, then 15, murdered Connor Barrett in Hemsby, Norfolk in 2014 - leading to both being jailed for life with a minimum term of 15 years.But a later change in the law meant Quaye could not ask for a review of that minimum term, because he had turned 18 before he was sentenced.The Supreme Court's decision to reject his appeal ends the legal battle over juvenile life sentences in the UK courts - but the case could potentially be reopened at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.Connor Barrett, 21, died after he was attacked by Quaye and Ayomindy Bile when they turned up uninvited at a birthday party to assault another attendee.Their trial heard that the pair had brought knives with them and that their victim died in front of his family, including his younger brother.After their conviction, Quaye, by then 18, and Bile were jailed at Her Majesty's pleasure - the legal term for a life sentence given to child killers.Under long-standing legal principles, a juvenile who is sentenced to murder can ask for their minimum term to be reconsidered once they have served half of that time.Image caption, Connor Barrett was killed while defending another party-goer That policy and other juvenile sentencing laws take into account evidence that some serious offenders rehabilitate in their 20s as they mature.However, Parliament voted in 2022 to block juvenile killers from seeking a review if they had been sentenced after they had turned 18.The new law meant Quaye could no longer ask for a review of his minimum term and the 29-year-old remains in prison, prompting him to mount a legal challenge.Lawyers for Quaye had argued that his treatment amounted to a breach of the ban on arbitrary detention, retrospective punishment and discrimination based on age in the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).In 2024, two High Court judges ruled that Quaye's treatment breached those safeguards - but the Court of Appeal later reversed that decision.In their ruling on Tuesday, the five Supreme Court judges said the law had long differentiated between child and adult killers, and that the trial judge had correctly and fairly decided on a minimum term.They concluded the ECHR did not compel the UK government to consider reducing Quaye's minimum term.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The Supreme Court resolves disputes over what the law means in the UK"The judgement is one of social policy, involving questions of moral and political judgement, which is the province of the legislature [Parliament]," they said."Moreover, drawing a bright line distinction based on being 18 at the date of conviction or sentence is a recognised feature of sentencing and the criminal justice system."Simon Creighton, a leading sentencing law solicitor who represented Quaye, said the case had raised two basic questions of fairness."When people receive these particular sentences, they were told that the sentence meant they would have a review," he said."To be told a decade later that was no longer the case is one aspect of the unfairness."We all know about the lengthy delays in the criminal courts at the moment. And it really is purely arbitrary whether your case is going to come up for trial before you've turned 18 or not."To make a decision about what the sentence means, based on something that's so arbitrary and out of people's control, feels like a major injustice."Creighton said there was a "strong prospect" of asking the European court in Strasbourg to review the outcome. In general, such cases can take years to be heard and the court only considers appeals when it thinks the courts in the UK have not fully resolved human rights questions.

schema.headline: Juvenile murder sentence rule doesn't breach human rights, says Supreme Court

title: Can you take the 'London' out of London Fashion Week?
description: The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different.Fashion Brita
body: The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different.Fashion Britain is the British Fashion Council's initiative to open up access to talent outside of London - so how do you shift the focus away from the traditional centre of that world?The council told BBC Newsbeat it has been working with LFW on a series of pop-up events in England, Wales and Scotland to show this year's event was "bigger than London". Northern Ireland wasn't included as a location for this year's initiative - but will be included next year, the council said. A recent House of Commons report, external found that more than half (51%) of the creative industries' economic output was generated in London in 2022.However, it did report that there are "clusters of creative industries" across the country, which included cities like Manchester and Leeds."A lot of people think in order to make it big, you have come to this big city because it has the schools here," says Charles Jeffrey, founder and creative director of international fashion label Loverboy. "But actually, there is so much amazing education that happens in different places," the Scottish designer tells Newsbeat."I first started [in] a tiny studio in Dalston [in east London] and we were having to use fabrics from these cheap fabric shops that you would probably only really get in London because of the rag trade," he recalls."Now a lot of them have gone and what made London a capital city for fashion has been taken away, so you're probably better getting your fabrics from a little fabric shop in Manchester - it's probably ten times cheaper."Jeffrey supported Fashion Britain this year, with the aim of opening doors in the industry for creatives outside of London, but how feasible will that be?Birmingham City University graduate Imarnie Bennett knows a bit about the struggle. She travelled to the capital to showcase her project with fellow BCU fashion graduates to an audience at Somerset House. "London is such a big city, it's really well known and there are lots of opportunities," says the 22-year-old.  "You hear Birmingham and it's a bit like, 'will they get us the same opportunities as London?', but I feel like Birmingham is becoming more noticed for what we do."Bennett says you can harness the power of being different."Even colours, some cities are brighter and warmer than others, so it changes people's perspectives on things," she says.Yet fellow designer Sean Pajarillo says he is hopeful about job opportunities because of how the technology and fashion industry is moving."The merging of industries is what's going to create new opportunities for someone in the future," says the 25-year-old.This is something that British designer Priya Ahluwalia believes is vital. "I do think there is a genuine issue with London being seen as the centre of the universe in terms of fashion," she says. "There is incredible talent from all over the UK, some of the best designers have come from the north, come from Wales, Scotland". Ahluwalia spoke to Newsbeat after showcasing her archive at Westfield Stratford City shopping centre as part of Fashion Week. The designer explained how practical help is important in helping talent access the industry."Whether we decentralise or not, London is still going to be the centre of UK fashion. "There needs to also be support for people to be able to travel to London, show up in London", Ahluwalia says.For Jeffrey, formal training isn't the only way into the fashion world."Sometimes having a university degree does kind of put your foot in the door - but honestly, I really think it's just about the work and work ethic."

schema.headline: Can you take the 'London' out of London Fashion Week?

title: Call of Duty's Activision to make next Halo game as Xbox cuts more jobs
description: Xbox is cutting hundreds of jobs and making sweeping changes to the production of its flagship Halo franchise, as its company-wide "reset" continues.I
body: Xbox is cutting hundreds of jobs and making sweeping changes to the production of its flagship Halo franchise, as its company-wide "reset" continues.Its latest reductions, forming part of a wave of ongoing layoffs, will impact staff at the studio which currently makes Halo - with Call of Duty publisher Activision to take on development of any future games.Jez Corden of Windows Central said the change was a "dramatic move", while gaming analyst Christopher Dring said it raised questions over whether it could help revive what was once Xbox's "crown jewel".It comes as questions also mount over the future of other notable Xbox studios, including Cambridge-based game developer Ninja Theory.Xbox chief executive Asha Sharma said in July the Bafta-winning studio behind the Hellblade games would be spun off, alongside four others, amid its dramatic downsizing. But Matt Booty, chief content officer at Xbox, wrote in a blog post on Tuesday, external that attempts to find a buyer for the studio had failed - with "two separate agreements" falling through.He said Ninja Theory would now enter into consultation with employees on a proposed closure, though potential buyout talks are continuing.Of the four other affected companies, three have now returned to management, while consultation for Arcane remains "under way", Booty added.Xbox's announcement of a further 268 cut jobs comes after Sharma revealed in July that the company was "beginning the most significant restructure in Xbox history".It saw 1,600 jobs cut immediately, amid 3,600 planned losses overall.The company says it is three quarters of the way through its planned restructure.Sharma said, external at the time that the Microsoft's gaming division had not been "healthy" and while platforms like its subscription plan Game Pass had "created meaningful value", they had not grown quickly enough.In an interview with the BBC in August, she also pointed to the "crisis" in rising computing prices and hardware costs as another external pressure on the company.Halo has been a hallmark of the Xbox brand since Microsoft's first entry into the console market in 2001, helping establish the firm as a major player in the industry.Xbox said on Tuesday that Halo Studios, which recently released Halo: Campaign Evolved in July, would continue to support the game's community and work on existing games, as opposed to focusing on any new release.Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, said the military sci-fi shooter was once Xbox's "crown jewel" but that hadn't been the case "for more than a decade"."Halo was once to Xbox what Mario is to Nintendo," said Corden, "but years of mismanagement have eroded that".Dring said bringing Halo under Activision's leadership "makes sense", though the company would be "mindful not to lose what makes Halo unique"."For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place" said Rob Kostich, Activision's president."We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community."As well as leading any new Halo game development, Xbox said Activision's remit would expand to manage the World's Edge studio, home to the Age of Empires franchise, as well as the studio Rare and its series Sea of Thieves.The PlayStation rival also confirmed consolidations of some of its current companies - saying Elder Scroll-makers Bethesda would "expand its remit" to include Fallout New Vegas-makers Obsidian, and combining the studios behind Forza Horizon and Fable.

schema.headline: Call of Duty's Activision to make next Halo game as Xbox cuts more jobs

title: Martha's Rule rolled out across all A&E departments in England
description: Elliott Paterson, from Cheltenham, told the BBC he "truly believes" Martha's Rule saved the life of his 67-year-old father, Chris, who was treated at
body: Elliott Paterson, from Cheltenham, told the BBC he "truly believes" Martha's Rule saved the life of his 67-year-old father, Chris, who was treated at Gloucester Royal Hospital last year after he broke four ribs falling off his bike.Elliott said his father's treatment in the surgical ward was complicated due to his Addison's disease, a rare autoimmune condition affecting the adrenal glands.The family noticed Chris' deterioration in health, Elliott said, and called the critical care team, which was then able to treat both Chris' injuries and his Addison's."To hear that Martha's Rule is now to be rolled out across the NHS is brilliant news and I hope that for more people it will continue to save lives," Elliott said."I am incredibly fortunate and grateful to have had Martha's Rule at our disposal at the time."During an eight-month pilot of the scheme at seven emergency departments, 69 calls were made to dedicated Martha's Rule phone numbers, including some calls relating to acute deterioration following an urgent clinical review. In some cases, it led to a patient having immediate surgery or being transferred to intensive care.Fowler told the BBC's Today programme that, while these numbers might seem relatively small, the decision to roll out Martha's Rule further was "on a background of very, very extensive experience in other settings". This included in-patient wards, where he said his teams had received "nearly 20,000 calls" - three quarters of which came from families.Fowler said: "Early testing has shown that Martha's Rule can work well in busy A&Es and builds on the evidence from our adult and children's wards, where thousands of calls have been made by patients, families and staff to date, with many leading to changes in treatment and potentially life-saving interventions."Questioned whether busy A&E staff might struggle with a sudden influx of calls, Fowler said this had not played out in the recent tests. "Actually people have used it very sensibly," he added. "We've tested it through winter and across this busy summer, and therefore I am not concerned that when we roll this out we are going to be overwhelmed with calls." Health minister Baroness Merron said the initiative was part of "wider efforts to put patient safety at the heart of the NHS".Actor Jason Watkins, whose two-and-a-half-year-old daughter Maude died from sepsis in 2011, praised the rollout, saying Martha's Rule was already "making a difference on the wards"."It enables a parent to have a voice and if there is an issue, that is addressed," he told BBC Breakfast, urging parents: "If you're at all worried when you go into A&E, ask for a second opinion."Watkins said the rollout of Martha's law could benefit medical professionals too, explaining: "Those extremely dedicated medical practitioners, nurses, doctors and consultants, it gives them a pause and a thought [of] 'am I doing everything I can to assess this child accurately?'."Before the phased rollout is completed in England, patients and their families can check with their local hospital or NHS trust where Martha's Rule is available by visiting the trust's website or asking hospital staff.

schema.headline: Martha's Rule rolled out across all A&E departments in England

title: Billie Jean King Cup 2026: Great Britain out as Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter lose to Czech Republic
description: Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter lost their respective singles matches as Great Britain were beaten by a strong Czech Republic side in the Billie Jean K
body: Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter lost their respective singles matches as Great Britain were beaten by a strong Czech Republic side in the Billie Jean King Cup quarter-finals.Anne Keothavong's team headed into the tie as underdogs, with all five Czech players placed higher in the singles rankings than any of the British squad.Sonay Kartal produced a gritty performance as she returned to tennis after six months out with a lower back injury, but fell to a narrow 7-6 (7-2) 4-6 6-4 defeat in a marathon three-hour encounter with Marie Bouzkova.Boulter could do little to get Britain back into the best-of-three tie as she was outplayed 6-2 7-6 (7-3) by Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.It was a second successive loss for Boulter at the hands of a Czech player, coming just three weeks after a 58-minute demolition by Karolina Muchova at the US Open.It is the first time since 2023 that Britain have failed to reach the semi-finals at the Billie Jean King Cup and their wait for a maiden title will go on for another year.The Czech Republic, who are 11-time winners of the tournament and the only team boasting two top-10 players at the Finals, will face either Kazakhstan or Spain in Friday's semi-finals.Playing her first match since retiring injured in the fourth round at Indian Wells in March, Kartal started well and struck early against world number 26 Bouzkova.However, she was broken back immediately and Bouzkova dominated the tie-break to take the opener.The Briton broke early in the second set and held on to force a decider, but her first double fault of the match handed Bouzkova a break for a 4-2 lead.Kartal delayed defeat by saving three match points and breaking back, but Bouzkova restored her lead immediately to clinch victory after exactly three hours on court to put the Czechs in front.With Noskova and Muchova - this year's Wimbledon finalists - in the Czech squad, it was always going to be a uphill battle for number one Boulter.Two double faults in the first game saw Boulter drop serve early and world number six Noskova steamrolled her way through the opening four games before wrapping up the set.Boulter improved in the second set and threatened to force a decider, but she was unable to create a single break point and Noskova took control of the tie-break to send her nation into the semi-finals.

title: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe
description: Young people can book to get their Men B vaccine at high street pharmacies across England. There are walk-in appointments too, external. Two doses off
body: Young people can book to get their Men B vaccine at high street pharmacies across England. There are walk-in appointments too, external. Two doses offer the best protection. First doses are available until 31 December 2026, with second doses available until 31 March 2027. Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in Pathogen Genomics at UKHSA, said: "This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change."The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place."Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she said bacteria are known to undergo changes like this, known as horizontal gene transfer.Such changes can make infections more severe, and may mean they get past the immune system because people haven't encountered them before. These events, while rare and unpredictable, could happen again, so experts "should not take their eye off the ball", she added. Scientists say speed and severity of the Kent outbreak was very unusual. It was described as "unprecedented" and "explosive" at the time, with so many infections happening in one place and over a very short period.Two people died - a 21-year-old University of Kent student and Juliette Kenny, a sixth-form pupil at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Faversham.The outbreak is thought to have started in a nightclub called Club Chemistry in the city centre, which was popular with university students.It's likely one person brought the infection in with them, and then it spread that evening. Meningitis is passed through close contact - including kissing and sharing drinks or vapes.  Dr Rodrigues suspects the very same genetic changes that made the strain so dangerous may also explain why the outbreak was short-lived and did not continue to spread.People were generally too sick to be silent carriers who can pass it on unknowingly to others.Prof Robert Heyderman, an expert in infectious diseases at University College London, said the outbreak strain could have been carried by healthy people for some time before the conditions were right for the outbreak to occur.Following the Kent outbreak, a one-off menB vaccination programme was launched to protect young people heading to university this autumn.Advisers, are asking the government to consider introducing MenB jabs routinely for secondary school-aged people at around the age of 15 to better protect them against a disease that can be deadly.Anyone concerned about symptoms of meningitis or sepsis, which can include fever, headache, stiff neck, sensitivity to light, a rash that does not fade under pressure, difficulty breathing and muscle pain should seek medical help immediately.

title: Mikel Arteta agrees new contract to extend stay as Arsenal manager
description: News of Arteta's agreement over a new deal at Arsenal won't come as a shock - but it is a major development nevertheless.The fact his existing deal ex
body: News of Arteta's agreement over a new deal at Arsenal won't come as a shock - but it is a major development nevertheless.The fact his existing deal expires at the end of the season did put a slightly greater emphasis on the speed of discussions than normal.But Arteta has been transparent about his desire to stay at the club beyond the end of this campaign.Dynasty building is what has driven Arteta's decision. Winning Arsenal's first Premier League title in 20 years last season is viewed as just the start.Coming within a penalty kick of winning their first Champions League trophy came as a gut-wrenching blow - but also a huge motivation.With that in mind, there was never a sense Arteta was preparing to walk away from the team he has built to become one of the best in European football.So with a deal for their manager to stay now agreed, the foundation of Arsenal's recent revitalisation into a footballing force remains in place.Does more history beckon? Arteta is committed to finding out.

schema.headline: Mikel Arteta agrees new contract to extend stay as Arsenal manager

title: Four people die in Bootle house fire
description: Image caption, Fire crews were called to the scene at 03:45 BST after receiving a 999 call ByLauren HirstNorth WestUpdated 31 minutes agoFour people h
body: Image caption, Fire crews were called to the scene at 03:45 BST after receiving a 999 call ByLauren HirstNorth WestUpdated 31 minutes agoFour people have died and a fifth has been taken to hospital with burns after a house fire on Merseyside.Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property in Stone Square in Bootle, Sefton, at 03:45 BST.Eight firefighters searched the house where they discovered four people in an upstairs bedroom, showing no signs of life, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said. Another casualty, who was outside the property when crews arrived, was taken to hospital.Officers from Merseyside Police are also at the scene and a joint investigation with the fire service into the cause of the blaze is under way. The North West Ambulance Service's hazardous area response team also attended the scene of the fire and confirmed the four fatalities.Chief Fire Officer Nick Searle confirmed the "intense fire [had] spread very rapidly".The street was cordoned off by police and, earlier, fire officers could be seen knocking on neighbours' doors.One said: "I heard shouting in the early hours but I just thought someone was having an argument, then I came downstairs and saw all the fire engines."Another local resident, who did not want to be named, said: "We all came out on the front and we could see smoke coming over from the houses."The sirens woke me up and there were fire engines in the street."The fire service said the main blaze had been extinguished with crews damping down the area.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The fifth casualty was outside the house when fire crews arrivedKevin Longshaw, area manager for Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service, said: "This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives and been injured. "We will work closely with relevant colleagues to ascertain the cause of the fire, but in the immediate term, we again extend our sincere condolences to those affected by this tragic incident."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Emergency services remain at the scene as investigations continue Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover on Merseyside

title: Henry Pollock: Eddie Hearn says back row 'left money on the table' with Northampton deal
description: Henry Pollock turned down rival offers worth hundreds of thousands of pounds more than his extension to stay at boyhood club Northampton, says Eddie H
body: Henry Pollock turned down rival offers worth hundreds of thousands of pounds more than his extension to stay at boyhood club Northampton, says Eddie Hearn.Hearn, whose Matchroom promotional empire is centred on boxing, darts and snooker, has been working as Pollock's adviser since March.Pollock, 21, has agreed a new deal with Saints that extends his terms to summer 2028 and is worth more than £400,000 a year."There were a couple of domestic offers – a couple of Prem offers - and international offers as well," said Hearn of Pollock's options during his renegotiation."We had a very, very straight conversation. I said to him, 'be honest, do you want to go?' And he went, 'no, I really don't want to go'. And that was it."He knew the numbers, but ultimately he just wanted to stay at the club."He left a lot of money on the table to stay with Northampton. But it wasn't even a tough decision for him."Hearn says that some of Pollock's suitors were offering "well in excess of seven figures".The £1m mark was where Hearn valued Pollock's annual salary prospects in an interview with the Daily Telegraph interview in August., externalHearn acknowledges that his client's new deal "didn't quite get to the number" that was targeted.The headline basic figure Pollock has accepted does not account for a signing bonus and various payments he receives for off-pitch work.And Hearn says that Pollock's endorsement deals have carried him comfortably over £1m in total annual earnings."Everybody from major financial institutions to household brands to performance brands to nutritional brands to wellness brands… I mean, there isn't really a sector that hasn't hasn't approached us about Henry Pollock," said Hearn.Pollock is keen to explore the possibility of representing Great Britain in rugby sevens at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.GB's qualification is far from certain after the programme went part-time and the team slipped from the top tier of the international circuit.The back row's new deal does not include the sort of dedicated time to train up for sevens that France captain Antoine Dupont took before Paris 2024, but the prospect has been raised with Saints."Our principal obligation is to perform for Northampton and to help them win championships," said Hearn."Part of the arrangement allows him to look at those kind of opportunities, but only with a sensible conversation with the club."Pollock's ability to maximise his on-pitch earnings in England is restricted by a £6.4m salary cap for Prem clubs.Each team is allowed one player whose salary is exempt from the calculations; however, players who move between top-tier teams can only qualify for such marquee status after two years with their new side.Hearn would scrap the cap entirely."Let the players earn," he said. "All they hear about is salary caps or one star player per team - marquee names or whatever you want to call it. You don't want that."You want to say to a young player, 'hey, come to rugby, you can be a superstar and you can earn a fortune'."You could have lost Pollock and it would have been a disaster for English rugby."The salary cap is designed to make the Prem sustainable and competitive, with similar systems in place in most major American sports.Players such as Pollock can supplement club earnings with a central England contract, worth about £150,000 a year, or one-off Test match fees.Still, some England players, such as Jack Willis, Kyle Sinckler and Sam Simmonds, have left for France's Top 14 where a salary cap of 11m euros (£9.4m) offers scope for greater earnings.Hearn's current stable of rugby stars is only two strong. Bath and Scotland fly-half Finn Russell is similarly represented by Matchroom in off-pitch matters and advised by Hearn.However, Hearn has ambitions to become more deeply involved in the staging and promotion of the game. He is set to meet with Prem Rugby chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor in Monaco in the coming weeks to discuss ideas."We haven't really touched the surface in terms of what we could do in the sport," said Hearn."All I've done is done a few deals with Henry, he's come to a couple of fights and I've done a couple of Zoom calls [with journalists]."That just shows you the buzz that can be created with a little bit of hype and perception."But hype and perception are nothing without substance. The sport and the brand is the substance and it's significant in rugby."Look at what Matchroom has done elsewhere. Boxing was dead, darts was non-existent, snooker was stuck in the air. We don't fail. Our track record is second to none."If we went into rugby, it would be a stroll in the park for me. It's a huge global sport steeped in history with fantastic values and tradition that just needs to be just turbo-charged."

schema.headline: Henry Pollock: Eddie Hearn says back row 'left money on the table' with Northampton deal
